newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Volcker asks Swiss to disclose Holocaust accounts.
newsitem.headline: Volcker asks Swiss to disclose Holocaust accounts.

text.p: The American investigator leading the hunt for dormant Swiss bank accounts of Jews murdered by Hitler urged the country's bankers on Thursday to publish the names of wartime account holders worldwide as soon as possible.
Paul Volcker, a former U.S. Federal Reserve chairman, heads an independent commission empowered by Swiss banks to waive banking secrecy rules in order to scrutinise wartime accounts.
He said the commission expected the names of holders of dormant accounts opened before 1945 to be published in the coming weeks -- including on the Internet.
"We've finally reached the stage of entering into banks," he told a news conference in Geneva.
"The recommendation of the committee to banking authorities in Switzerland is that a list of names for dormant accounts to be made available rapidly and to be published," he said.
"That must be disseminated as widely as possible so that potential claimants can have the list before them."

The disclosure will help inquiries into the wartime period led by Volcker's committee, which is overseeing an audit of banks aimed at returning any money found in Swiss bank vaults to Holocaust survivors or the heirs of the victims.
Jewish groups accuse Switzerland of hoarding the wealth of Holocaust victims and clearing looted Nazi gold.
The landlocked Alpine country's wartime neutrality in the midst of embattled Europe has come under international criticism as little more than collaboration with Nazis under a different name.
"It's interesting what you may find in archives. The Germans and the Swiss have been meticulous bookkeepers," Volcker said.
He said the investigation covered all assets including safe deposit boxes in the vaults of secretive Swiss banks.

"It has been suggested to me that at least in some cantons in Switzerland...there would have been a legal procedure to open safe deposit boxes after a lapse of time. The assets themselves should presumably be preserved," he said.
Volcker said his commission, which first came into being a year ago amid mounting international criticism of Switzerland's wartime past, was two months behind schedule.

"There's a lot of emotion attached to this, a lot of controversy, a lot of concern on both sides. I'm disappointed but it's perfectly natural for me to be disappointed in any effort of this kind," Volcker said.

But he said the work, which entails sifting through row upon row of wartime archives, should be finished on schedule by the end of 1998. "Our intention is to complete the whole thing next year. I'd hope by the end of next year, we'd be finished."
Tracing accounts that were supposed to be dormant but have been removed in the past 50 years, and Jewish money deposited on the names of third parties, was the main challenge, he said.

"What makes this difficult is the passage of 50 years, combined with a feeling that many of these refugee accounts would have been deposited by a third party and that third party may often, and typically, have been Swiss. The presumption is most of the names will be Swiss," Volcker said.
"I don't think this exercise has any credibility in the eyes of the Jewish community and the American community in general unless there is verification."
Auditors searching dormant accounts have selected five banks in an initial pilot project. A full-scale hunt among more banks will begin after a review of the pilot results in September.
The five are Credit Suisse, Swiss Bank Corporation, Spar and Leihkasse Berne, Bank Cantonale Vaudoise and Geneva private bank Pictet & Cie.
For claimants of dormant accounts, Volcker said there would be special procedures and "relaxed standards" against the normal Swiss practice to ensure rapid payment but did not elaborate.
"We feel that should get moving as quickly as possible if necessary on a voluntary basis," he said.
